stories.title: Nvidia Cuts Off Southeast Asia to Prove It Controls Its Chips
stories.story:
The story begins with a scandal, then becomes a supply-chain reckoning. On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO after reports emerged of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed — a Singapore cloud company that US investigators believe illegally funneled advanced AI chips to China. The mechanism was elegant and, until recently, perfectly legal: Chinese firms rented computing time at overseas data centers, never taking title to the chips but effectively using them for frontier AI work. Washington had long looked the other way. It stopped looking.

The Commerce Department published a new rule on November 16, effective November 19, that closes the cloud loophole by requiring export licenses for advanced chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. Nvidia's board, scrambling to show regulators it was serious, took direct control of export compliance. It then instructed Dell and Supermicro — the partners that actually assemble its chips into servers — to freeze all deliveries to buyers in the four Southeast Asian countries. Huang was reinstated as CEO on November 23; the day after, Washington added Megaspeed and six other companies to its Entity List.

The freeze hits a region that had been riding a genuine AI infrastructure boom. Malaysia and Indonesia in particular had attracted billions of dollars in data-center investment precisely because they offered legal, US-allied geography from which to access Nvidia's best hardware. That geography is now a liability. One server maker has already begun pivoting its Southeast Asian order book toward Japan and South Korea. Meanwhile, lenders have reportedly paused billions in financing tied to Chinese cloud providers in the region.

The deeper implication is structural: US export controls have finally caught up with the workaround they were always meant to close. The question is whether Southeast Asia's legitimate AI ambitions — separate entirely from China's — will be collateral damage while the licensing bureaucracy catches up.
stories.hook: The cloud loophole that let Chinese labs rent their way around chip bans just got closed — and Southeast Asia's data-center boom is caught in the crossfire.

stories.title: The FCC Just Moved the Data Center Off Earth
stories.story:
Every data center ever built has shared one constraint: gravity. It needs land, grid power, cooling water, and a permit from someone who doesn't want it in their backyard. On Wednesday, the FCC erased that assumption — at least on paper — by granting SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy up to one million Starmind satellites in low Earth orbit, explicitly designed to function as AI data centers in space. It is the first approval of its kind in U.S. regulatory history.

The logic SpaceX pitched to the FCC is not science fiction. AI computing is voracious; terrestrial data centers now consume roughly 2% of global electricity and face compounding backlash over water use and local grid strain. Starmind satellites, SpaceX argued, would run on near-continuous solar power, beam processed results to Earth via laser links to the existing Starlink network, and sidestep the whole land-and-cooling problem entirely. The FCC agreed enough to issue a license — though the approval comes loaded with conditions. SpaceX must fly its first operational Starmind satellite by 2033, reach 100,000 by 2035, and hit the full million by 2040. Debris rules for satellites above 600 kilometers remain unresolved, covering four of the six approved orbital shells.

The deeper consequence is competitive. Amazon — which opposed the application, calling SpaceX's timeline fantasy — is building its own orbital computing effort, as are Google and Blue Origin. The FCC's approval hands SpaceX a head start in what may become the defining infrastructure race of the next decade: who controls the compute layer above the clouds. If the physics and economics prove out, the question of where AI thinks will have a new answer — roughly 500 kilometers up.
stories.hook: The next fight over data center permits might be settled not by a city council, but by an orbital debris plan.

stories.title: Washington Names Overproduction a Trade Crime, Hits 14 Partners
stories.story:
On the eve of Thanksgiving, the Trump administration dropped a document that trade lawyers will be reading for months: a proposed set of Section 301 tariffs on 14 major trading partners — China, the EU, Japan, India, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia, Bangladesh, Singapore, and Switzerland — all accused of the same offense: structural excess industrial capacity.

The legal scaffolding matters. Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act lets Washington punish countries it determines are treating U.S. businesses unfairly. The USTR spent eight months investigating alleged overproduction across industries from steel and automobiles to semiconductors and solar panels. The conclusion, applied to nearly every major export economy on earth, was that subsidized factories were pumping out more goods than their own markets could absorb — and that the resulting glut was landing on American shores, undercutting domestic producers.

China faces the sharpest edge. The proposed 20% excess-capacity tariffs would layer on top of the roughly 25% tariffs still in place from Trump's first term, potentially pushing total duties above 45%. For the EU, Japan, and others, rates are expected to range from 10% to 18%, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer signaled these are targeted, not blanket, levies — meaning specific goods rather than everything a country exports.

The timing is deliberate pressure, not recklessness. Rates will not take effect for months, giving trading partners a runway to negotiate. That is the mechanism: announce the threat, open the room. But the countries targeted — which include almost every significant U.S. ally in Asia and Europe — are running out of room to maneuver. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after November's midterms found 62% of Americans would support repealing earlier tariffs, suggesting the domestic political cost of this strategy is quietly rising even as the White House doubles down.
stories.hook: When you define excess production as a trade crime, you have essentially made economic efficiency itself negotiable.

stories.title: S&P Puts Nvidia on Downgrade Watch Over Board It Cannot Trust
stories.story:
Credit ratings are supposed to measure the ability to repay debt. Governance — who runs the company and whether anyone can hold them accountable — is usually a soft footnote. This week, S&P Global Ratings made it the headline.

S&P placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on CreditWatch with negative implications, warning it could cut the chipmaker by one notch to AA- within 90 days. The trigger was not a bad earnings report. Nvidia's financials remain formidable. The trigger was the board: specifically, its decision to fire Jensen Huang, then reverse course and reinstate him days later after the White House weighed in — a sequence that exposed, in S&P's words, deficiencies in management oversight, weak board independence, long-tenured directors, and no credible succession plan.

The mechanics of why this matters extend far beyond Nvidia's own borrowing costs. Nvidia has quietly become a credit backstop for the broader AI infrastructure ecosystem — the neoclouds and hyperscale infrastructure firms that lack strong credit ratings of their own. When these companies borrow to build out data centers, lenders have pressed Nvidia to backstop or guarantee more of that debt. A downgrade tightens those chains: collateral requirements rise, lending spreads widen, and AI build-out gets incrementally more expensive at precisely the moment demand is soaring.

Moody's took a softer line, calling Huang's return a stabilizing development that reduces near-term uncertainty. But S&P's harder read points to something structural: the board told investors it would not rehire Huang because his conduct was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct — then did exactly that. At his first all-hands back, Huang told staff a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy. S&P noticed.

The irony is clean: Nvidia's market power is so concentrated in one person that his return both reassured markets and confirmed the governance risk that caused the problem in the first place.
stories.hook: The board said it wouldn't rehire him — then did — and now the credit agency is asking who exactly is in charge.
stories.source: S&P Global Ratings / CNBC / Bloomberg, November 26, 2026

stories.title: The Fed's Dilemma: Growth at 4.3%, Inflation Still Won't Quit
stories.story:
On the eve of Thanksgiving, the U.S. government handed Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh an unusually clean set of numbers — and an unusually ugly problem. Third-quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3% annualized, well above the 3.5% forecast. At the same time, October's core PCE inflation print came in at 3.3% year-on-year, above expectations, while personal income surged 0.7% against a 0.4% forecast. The economy, in other words, is running hot on every dial at once.

The mechanism matters here. Strong income growth feeds consumer spending, which feeds services inflation — the stickiest kind. The Fed cannot wish this away by waiting. Markets know it: Polymarket traders now put the odds of a December rate hike at 93.5%, and CME's FedWatch prices in a 60% chance of a larger 50-basis-point move in January. The 10-year Treasury yield has anchored near 4.85%, a level that makes mortgage debt painful and corporate refinancing expensive.

What makes this genuinely consequential is the global echo. The Bank of Korea hiked 25 basis points to 3.25% today and lifted its 2027 growth forecast to 4.1%, citing a chip-export boom — but that optimism is conditional on U.S. demand staying strong. Meanwhile Brent crude is pushing $95 a barrel after Houthi strikes on Saudi ports, adding a fresh inflation layer just as central banks worldwide are trying to declare victory. The Fed's December meeting is now less a question of if than by how much — and every emerging market with dollar-denominated debt will feel the answer.
stories.hook: An economy growing at 4.3% while inflation refuses to fall isn't a success story — it's the Fed's nightmare.
stories.source: Tickmill / Rio Times / CME FedWatch, November 26 2026
